stops.name: Gabès, the last defeat
stops.campa: The armies meet near Gabès, on the coastal road where the Numidian kings once held their salt-lake frontier, and this time Hassan's reinforced host does not break. Whole companies of her own confederation, worn down by five years of scorched fields, either fail her in the field or have already gone over; one telling even preserves an old officer of Kusayla's own line fighting now against her. Dihya's line is broken by evening. She does not surrender the field; she leaves it, riding for the only ground left that has never betrayed her: the Aurès itself.

stops.name: The retreat road, 'monarchs do not flee from death'
stops.campa: On the road back into the mountain her own captains beg her to keep riding, to scatter into country too broken for Hassan's cavalry to follow, to live. She refuses in the words the tradition keeps as her last recorded defiance: she is a queen, and queens do not run from death. She turns her diminished companies to make what stand the ground allows, choosing the manner of the end over the postponement of it, the same clarity, the register insists, that let her read every battlefield for five years now turned at last upon her own.
stops.quote: How can I leave and flee when I am a queen? Monarchs do not flee from death, and how can I bring shame upon my people for all eternity?
stops.quote_source: al-Zāwī's account of her refusal to retreat, as carried in Kahina (en.wikipedia)

stops.name: Bir al-Kahina, the well that keeps her name
stops.campa: Hassan's cavalry runs her companies down in the borderland between the Aurès and the desert, at a well the country will call Bir al-Kahina from this day on and still calls it now, thirteen centuries later. The chroniclers do not agree on the manner of the end: sword in hand, most say; some say by her own poison rather than capture, but they agree she is killed there and beheaded on the spot, the well becoming the one fixed point the whole disputed legend can be hung from. The Aurès has lost its oracle and its queen in the same afternoon.

stops.name: Damascus, the head before the Caliph
stops.campa: Her head is carried the whole width of the conquest, from the Aurès to Damascus, and laid before Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan as the promised proof that the Kahina's war is finished, the very scene, the tradition insists, that she had already seen in her own dream and had already told her sons was coming. Whether the Caliph receives it as triumph, or, as some later tellings soften it, as the melancholy proof of an enemy worth respecting, the register does not choose. What the whole Maghreb now knows is that the mountain's five years are over, and the invasion, delayed as long as one woman could delay it, resumes.

stops.name: Kairouan, the sons received
stops.campa: Hassan welcomes her sons and her adopted Khalid exactly as the dream foretold: not as hostages but as officers, converted and commissioned, given command over Berber troops within the very army that killed their mother. It is remembered two ways at once, as the register keeps both: a conqueror's shrewdness, binding the defeated confederation to himself through her own blood, and the fulfillment of a mother's last calculation, that her line and her people would outlast her by joining what she could not defeat. Twelve thousand Berbers, some from her own confederation, are enrolled under the new peace.

stops.name: The Straits, her people's sons cross into Iberia
stops.campa: Eight years after her death, Berber troops raised from the very confederations she once led cross the narrow water under Tariq ibn Ziyad, the rock where he lands keeping his own name into the present, Jabal Tariq. Some tellings go further and make Tariq himself her kinsman, even her son, by another accounting, a claim the register cannot confirm but records as part of what the legend has grown to hold. Whatever the truth of that claim, it is her people's spears, not the Arabs' alone, that open Spain, the last irony of a war she fought to keep them free of any empire at all.

stops.name: Kabylia, Lalla Fatma n'Soumer takes up the mountain's old office
stops.campa: More than eleven centuries on, the mountains answer a second time to a woman the country calls prophetess. Lalla Fatma n'Soumer leads the Kabyle resistance against a new invader, the French, from strongholds in the Djurdjura ranges that once sheltered the Aurès confederation's western kin; it takes an army of thirty thousand to put her down in 1857. The register does not claim her as Dihya's blood, only as the mountain's habit: that when North Africa's plain surrenders, its highlands produce, again, a woman who will not.

stops.name: Baghaï, the statue raised, burned, and mended
stops.campa: In 2003, on the same ground she once ordered razed, the Association Aurès El-Kahia raises a statue of Dihya in Baghaï's town square, the queen remembered exactly where the queen once burned a town for her people's sake. On the night of 12 April 2016 unnamed arsonists set the statue alight, a small violence answering a larger argument still unresolved: whose heroine she is, and what her memory is for. Within days young Chaoui from the mountain restore her, unasked: the same local devotion that first kept her name alive when no chronicle would.

stops.name: Tizi Ouzou: the mural, and the name still spoken
stops.campa: On a wall outside Tizi Ouzou, in the heart of Kabylia, a mural sets Dihya beside Massinissa and Jugurtha, three Imazighen resisters, one of them a woman, claimed together as the deep root of a people the Arabic chronicles once tried to erase and the French colonial pen once tried to annex for its own argument. The Amazigh flag she is painted beside, blue for the sea, green for the mountain, yellow for the desert, the red tifinagh letter for the free man at its center, flies now over a living movement that reads her, still, as its oldest face.
